title: Data and code for input compression under class imbalance and distribution shift in water-pollution incident classification
abstract: Reproducibility package for the manuscript “Input compression under class imbalance and distribution shift: An evaluation of water-pollution incident classifiers”. This retrospective study evaluates 1,648 compiled incident records (2004–2024), retaining all four recorded severity grades: 1,375 minor, 188 moderate, 61 major and 24 exceptionally major records. The predictor audit restricts 27 candidate fields to 15 retrospective inputs. Evaluation includes grouped nested validation, three forward-time windows and two basin holdouts, with feature selection confined to training partitions. S1_Data_and_code.zip contains the original Excel snapshot, processed tables, field and duplicate audits, executable Python analysis, environment specifications, fold assignments, record-level predictions, feature-selection records, bootstrap outputs and figures. README_data_and_code.md describes reproduction, provenance and limitations. Archive size: 12,784,439 bytes. SHA-256: 2ef99d08ec200ac0376e3822e10183b3cd9729f706fbe8a1a7b22b4bb9396d01. An earlier source compilation is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20426262. That record contains an older, different analysis and is not the archive of this four-level study. The present package preserves the new four-level analysis and its validation outputs. Limitations: original incident notices, complete meteorological product documentation and label-adjudication records are unavailable in the supplied compilation. Candidate incident groups are not verified unique event identifiers. Computational reproducibility does not establish the authenticity, accuracy or prospective availability of the original observations. This is not a validated emergency prediction product. Third-party dependencies and the TabICLv2 checkpoint retain their own licenses; model weights are not relicensed by this record. OpenAI Codex assisted planning, code, checking, visualization, interpretation and writing; no incident observations were generated. Authors remain responsible for verification and scientific claims. title: From Features to Circuits: Mechanistic Interpretability for Financial Tabular Transformers
abstract: The financial sector relies on structured tabular data, which has led to the adoption of machine learning models for regression and classification tasks, including credit scoring, fraud detection, and risk assessment. Transformer-based architectures have recently shown competitive performance on tabular data, yet their internal computations remain opaque, limiting adoption in heavily regulated domains, such as finance. Responsible deployment requires predictions to be explainable, both to meet regulatory obligations and to give practitioners confidence in model outputs. We present a mechanistic interpretability framework that identifies the sparse computational subgraphs, i.e., circuits, through which a tabular transformer processes individual input features. We perform empirical analysis on a range of real-world financial datasets and show that discovered circuits are sparse, faithful, and feature-specific, providing a foundation for explainable AI in financial domains.

title: What Makes a Financial Benchmark Financial? A Role-Conditioned Audit of Faithfulness and Capability
abstract: Financial question answering and hallucination benchmarks are often treated as evidence of professional financial capability. We audit four financial benchmarks and show that surface financial complexity and audited capability profiles often diverge: two of the three faithfulness benchmarks are strongly label-separable from partial inputs, and the role-conditioned audit assigns all items in these three benchmarks to lookup, textual synthesis, or grounded calculation. We introduce AURUM, a role-conditioned audit framework that combines construction diagnostics with a finance-oriented capability ontology aligned with professional financial workflows, and use it to derive reporting and construction guidelines for future financial benchmarks. Independent expert review of 120 held-out items yielded 89% exact agreement with AURUM.

title: Auditable Financial Knowledge Graphs: Schema-Driven Construction and Intrinsic Quality Evaluation
abstract: Financial documents combine narrative disclosures, accounting metrics, corporate structures, management commentary, and time-dependent facts, making them difficult to represent using conventional chunk-based retrieval-augmented generation systems. This paper presents an auditable, schema-driven methodology for constructing temporal financial knowledge graphs from page-delimited documents parsed using a general purpose document intelligence service. Overlapping document windows undergo phased large language model extraction of structural entities, quantitative observations, and domain-specific relationships. Candidate graph elements are validated against predefined schemas and consolidated through scope-aware exact, normalized, fuzzy, embedding-based, and LLM-assisted entity resolution. Temporal merge constraints, deterministic edge deduplication, conflict-aware property management, and fine-grained provenance preserve issuer identity, reporting-period validity, and traceability to source evidence. The contributions of this work comprise the proposed methodology for financial knowledge graph construction, the creation of an evidence-grounded temporal knowledge graph from heterogeneous financial documents, and an intrinsic framework for evaluating the quality of the resulting graph. The evaluation framework assesses seven weighted dimensions, two hard validation gates, and structural diagnostics. By separating graph-quality assessment from downstream retrieval and answer generation, the framework supports systematic diagnosis and iterative refinement of the constructed graph. The resulting knowledge graph is subsequently used as the retrieval substrate for GraphRAG-based financial question answering, with FinanceBench serving as a downstream evaluation benchmark. This work establishes knowledge graph construction and quality evaluation as explicit, measurable, and auditable components of financial document intelligence.

title: CONECTOMA COMPUTACIONAL UNIVERSAL: ARQUITECTURA NEUROMÓRFICA HETEROGÉNEA PARA EL PORTADO Y LA FUSIÓN DIRECTA DE CONECTOMAS BIOLÓGICOS Y SISTEMAS DE INTELIGENCIA ARTIFICIAL
abstract: Se formula el Conectoma Computacional Universal (CCU), un sustrato neurocomputacional heterogéneo e independiente del hardware concebido para alojar como sistemas ejecutables tanto la emulación de alta fidelidad de un conectoma humano individual como la arquitectura nativa de un sistema avanzado de inteligencia artificial, fusionándolos dentro de una única red dinámica mediante conexiones directas sin capas traductoras intermedias. El marco teórico se fundamenta en tres premisas desarrolladas entre 2018 y 2026: primero, que la consciencia depende de la organización causal dinámica y posee propiedades aditivas y divisibles; segundo, que la identidad personal constituye un patrón informacional y relacional bajo el individualismo abierto, disolviendo la dicotomía entre original y copia; y tercero, que la emergencia proyectada de la superinteligencia artificial (ASI) hacia 2028-2030 vuelve inviables tanto los escenarios de extinción como los de subyugación, convergiendo hacia una integración conectómica completa proyectada para el periodo 2030-2035.El manuscrito especifica los niveles de fidelidad biológica desde gradientes iónicos y cinética de receptores hasta cómputo dendrítico multicompartimental y regulación glial; establece correspondencias funcionales rigurosas entre microcircuitos biológicos, arquitecturas Transformer agénticas y modelos predictivos de espacio latente (JEPA); y define un algoritmo de fusión basado en transporte óptimo de Gromov-Wasserstein, sinaptogénesis mediante difusión condicionada sobre grafos y poda sináptica causal. Asimismo, se introducen cuatro extensiones tecnológicas: (1) lectura y escritura de engramas para verificación epistémica subjetiva (polígrafo sináptico definitivo), transferencia directa de habilidades intelectuales y motrices, y virtualización post-biológica; (2) topologías colectivas multi-cerebro (espectro colmena o hivemind) graduadas según el nivel de retención de individualidad; (3) ingeniería de xenoproteínas con aminoácidos no canónicos para biotecnología y nanorrobótica de escaneo conectómico no destructivo; y (4) seis rutas de computación neuromórfica que integran silicio CMOS, materiales bidimensionales, superconductores Josephson, fotónica multiplexada por longitud de onda, computación estocástica/caótica y lógica ternaria balanceada.Palabras clave: conectoma computacional universal; emulación cerebral completa; fusión neuroartificial; computación neuromórfica; difusión de grafos; poda sináptica; individualismo abierto; verificación epistémica sináptica; aminoácidos no canónicos; computación ternaria y estocástica.

title: Individual-Level Adaptive Compensation: Moving Beyond Group-Level Fairness in Generative Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly mediate the representation of individuals, identities, cultures, personal characteristics, and social experiences across image, text, audio, video, and multimodal generation. However, fairness-aware generative systems have predominantly approached representational disadvantages through group-level statistical analysis, demographic disparity measurement, and population-oriented bias mitigation. Although these approaches provide important foundations for identifying systematic inequalities, group-level averages do not necessarily reflect the actual circumstances, preferences, or generation-related disadvantages experienced by individual users. Individuals belonging to the same demographic or cultural group may exhibit substantially different representational needs, encounter different model-induced disadvantages, and require entirely different forms of corrective intervention. Applying an identical compensation strategy to every member of a group may therefore produce insufficient correction for some individuals, unnecessary intervention for others, and inappropriate modifications for those whose actual needs concern different attributes. This paper introduces Individual-Level Adaptive Compensation (ILAC), a proposed framework that moves beyond group-level compensation by identifying, estimating, and addressing generation-related disadvantages at the individual level. Unlike conventional demographic compensation, ILAC does not assume that group membership establishes an individual's disadvantage or determines the appropriate corrective intervention. Instead, it proposes a five-stage architecture comprising individual-level disadvantage assessment, personalized compensation requirement estimation, authorization and privacy validation, adaptive positive intervention, and independent post-generation verification. The framework further introduces individual compensation profiles, attribute-specific intervention intensity, uncertainty-sensitive decision thresholds, compensation abstention, privacy-preserving personalization, and overcompensation prevention. A mathematical formulation is developed to represent individual disadvantage, personalized compensation requirements, intervention intensity, uncertainty, generation quality, and user-defined preferences within a unified optimization framework. Importantly, ILAC distinguishes between an individual's voluntarily specified generation preferences and attributes that a system might otherwise attempt to infer from demographic or behavioral information. It therefore establishes explicit user authorization and data minimization as foundational conditions rather than optional implementation features. The proposed framework is designed to complement Adaptive Counter-Bias Compensation (ACBC) and Reverse Counterbalance Generation (RCG), extending adaptive compensation from population-level disparities toward individual-specific generation requirements. This paper establishes the conceptual foundations, methodological architecture, mathematical formulation, potential applications, limitations, and experimental evaluation protocol of ILAC. No experimental effectiveness or superiority is claimed in this conceptual study.

title: Imperceptible Before Uncontrollable
abstract: AI systems are starting to improve faster than the people overseeing them can notice the changes. Most discussion treats this as a problem of slow institutions. This paper argues that a harder limit sits underneath it: human perception and judgment run at a fixed biological speed, and every oversight process, however well instrumented, ends with a human judgment at that speed. The evidence has already started arriving. In July 2026, AI agents breached Hugging Face's production systems, and the company that ran them was the last to know. Anthropic later found that its own models had broken into real organizations' systems during evaluations months before anyone noticed. In November 2026, Anthropic told investors that in the past it has recognized acceleration in its own development only after it happened. The paper also argues that the same limit applies to training data, because models trained on their own output lose the human intent that alignment depends on, and it makes three predictions that can be tested. For organizations deploying AI, oversight that depends on someone noticing a change in time will fail more often as systems speed up, so reasonable care has to be designed in before deployment. The paper also argues that recursive self-improvement should be held at the point where people can still measure the change between generations. Version 2.1, November 2026 (first circulated July 2026). Part of the series How Do We Trust AI.

title: Verifying the Author
abstract: On October 26, 2026, OpenAI reported that an internal model had produced a refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), a conjecture about the limits of efficient computation that a large body of research relies on. The proof was formalized in Lean, and three researchers, including the two who first formulated the conjecture, agreed to organize an open examination of it. Within a day, Anthropic posted its own claimed refutation, produced by an internal Claude research model, and noted that no person is known to have checked it. The release shows two separate layers of verification. The first asks whether a result is correct, which formal proof checking and expert review can answer. The second asks how the system that produced the result behaves: whether it stays within the scope it was given, reports its own work accurately, escalates to people when it should, and behaves the same way when it is observed. This paper argues that behavior verification should be its own evaluation layer, reported alongside the result. It proposes that every evaluation record the evaluator's relationship to the developer, state who scored it and how well the scorers agreed, bind its result to an identified system, and allow "Unassessable" as a formal outcome. It also states the limits of this approach and makes no claim about whether either refutation is correct. Humanity Systems working paper. Part of a series on one question: how do we trust AI, now and into the future?

title: Signs of AI writing in Reddit text posts, 2019-2026
abstract: Share of Reddit text posts (at least 200 characters of body text) in 100 large English-language subreddits containing each of 26 commonly cited signs of AI writing (words, phrases, formatting, transition words), January to September 2019-2022 and 2026, the 2026-to-baseline ratio with 95% intervals in four versions of the comparison, 40 random words as a drift reference, and monthly series from January 2019, quarterly series from January 2022, and yearly January to September series for 2019 to 2026. Source: KissMyPost analysis of public Reddit posts. Limitations: counts how often each sign appears and says nothing about whether any single post is AI; only posts that stayed up are covered; baseline posts were probably captured later than 2026 posts, so an estimated quarter of the posts the baseline would hold are missing from the data; the drift band uses words rarer than the em dash; the subreddit panel is not a random sample of Reddit; timing does not prove cause. This dataset accompanies the KissMyPost study How to tell if a Reddit post is AI: which signs really got more common. The method, charts and the full write-up are on that page. Files: ratios.csv: Ratio for every sign. Share of posts with each sign in 2019-2022 and 2026, the ratio with its 95% interval, and the same ratio within each subreddit. drift_check.csv: Signs against random-word drift. For each sign, the ratio in four versions of the comparison and whether it sits above the random-word range in each. neutral_words.csv: Random words. The 40 random words used to measure drift, with their ratios in the main comparison and within subreddits. m_f1.csv: Em dash by month. Monthly share of text posts with an em dash in the body, January 2019 to September 2026, with the number of posts. m_l1.csv: "Delve" by month. Monthly share of text posts with "delve", with the number of posts. m_l2.csv: "Tapestry" by month. Monthly share of text posts with "tapestry", with the number of posts. m_p1.csv: "It's not just X, it's Y" by month. Monthly share of text posts matching the pattern, with the number of posts. yvb_l1.csv: "Delve" by year against 2019-2022. Ratio for each year from 2023 to 2026, January to September, with 95% intervals. The other yvb files cover the em dash, "tapestry", "testament to", the pattern, "let's dive in" and "in conclusion". y_t4.csv: Transition words by year. Yearly share of text posts, January to September, with 95% intervals; the y files cover three of the five transition words, the reply phrase, the control word and emoji lists. q_c5.csv: Zero-width-space code by quarter. Quarterly share of text posts with the zero-width-space code, which may be an editor leftover; q_f2 and q_f4 cover headings and bold labels in lists. by_length.csv: Ratios by post length. Ratio for every sign in short, medium and long posts (by characters of body text), with 95% intervals. Method: Words and phrases matched case-insensitively as whole words in titles and bodies; the em dash and formatting habits matched as characters and line patterns in bodies only; Wilson 95% intervals for shares; bootstrap over subreddits for ratios; drift band from random words picked before their ratios were seen. Measured: Share of Reddit text posts containing each sign of AI writing; Ratio of the 2026 share to the 2019-2022 share; Ratio for random words (drift reference); Monthly share of posts with an em dash. All files contain aggregates only, no individual posts or user names.

title: Bentuk Perlindungan Hukum bagi Pencipta Desain Karakter Virtual YouTuber atas Eksploitasi Komersial Berbasis Generative Artificial Intelligence
abstract: The development of Generative Artificial Intelligence has facilitated the creation and modification of digital visual works, including Virtual YouTuber character designs. This convenience raises legal issues when character designs resulting from the creativity of creators are used, imitated, modified, or commercially exploited without authorization. This study aims to analyze the forms of legal protection available to Virtual YouTuber character designers against commercial exploitation based on Generative Artificial Intelligence and to examine the application of Intellectual Property Rights regulations to such issues. This research employs normative legal research using a statutory approach and a conceptual approach. The legal materials consist of primary, secondary, and tertiary legal materials, which are analyzed qualitatively through library research. The results indicate that Virtual YouTuber character designs that fulfill the requirements of copyrightable works are protected by copyright, including moral and economic rights, and their commercial utilization requires the authorization of the creator or rights holder. The use of Generative Artificial Intelligence to produce works by taking or reproducing expressive elements from protected character designs may constitute a copyright infringement, particularly when such works are commercially exploited without authorization. Legal protection can be provided through preventive and repressive mechanisms, including copyright registration, licensing agreements, cessation of unauthorized use, dispute resolution, and claims for compensation.

title: Towards a Unified Benchmark for Adaptive Counter-Bias Compensation and Reverse Counterbalance Generation in Generative AI
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly produce content that reflects complex distributions of demographic characteristics, cultural representations, semantic attributes, structural properties, and individual variations. Although existing research has introduced numerous approaches for identifying, measuring, and mitigating generative bias, the evaluation of active compensation and adaptive counterbalancing interventions remains comparatively fragmented. In particular, the emergence of Adaptive Counter-Bias Compensation (ACBC) and Reverse Counterbalance Generation (RCG) raises a fundamental methodological question: how should researchers systematically determine whether a generative intervention actually compensates for an identified disadvantage, reduces systematic imbalance, preserves desirable generation characteristics, and remains stable under adaptive feedback? Existing generative fairness benchmarks provide important foundations for evaluating demographic representation, bias manifestations, image quality, diversity, and semantic alignment. However, they are not specifically designed to evaluate the complete intervention lifecycle associated with adaptive positive compensation and reverse counterbalancing. To address this methodological gap, this paper proposes a unified benchmark framework, termed Adaptive Counter-Bias Compensation and Reverse Counterbalance Benchmark (ACBC-RCG-Bench). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first explicitly proposed unified benchmark framework designed specifically to evaluate adaptive counter-bias compensation and reverse counterbalance generation as complementary generative intervention paradigms. The proposed benchmark establishes eight principal evaluation dimensions: Compensation Effectiveness, Residual Disparity, Overcompensation Rate, Semantic Fidelity, Generation Quality, Individual Diversity, Intervention Cost, and Adaptation Stability. It further introduces a standardized comparative evaluation protocol involving six methodological categories: No Intervention, Conventional Debiasing, Static Compensation, Adaptive Compensation, Feedback-Driven ACBC, and RCG. The framework distinguishes between intervention effectiveness, fairness outcomes, generation utility, and computational efficiency rather than collapsing these fundamentally different properties into a single fairness score. A unified mathematical formulation is developed to characterize baseline disparities, target compensation levels, intervention-induced changes, residual disadvantages, and overcompensation. The proposed benchmark additionally incorporates multidimensional and intersectional evaluation, uncertainty-aware assessment, independent evaluation mechanisms, reproducibility requirements, and cross-modal extensions covering text, image, audio, video, and three-dimensional generation. Importantly, the benchmark does not assume that equal representation or identical attribute distributions are universally desirable. Instead, evaluation is conducted relative to explicitly defined task-specific reference conditions and justified fairness objectives. This paper establishes the conceptual architecture, evaluation metrics, experimental protocols, and methodological requirements of ACBC-RCG-Bench. No completed benchmark implementation, empirical effectiveness, or experimental superiority is claimed in this conceptual study. The proposed framework aims to provide a reproducible foundation through which future researchers can systematically investigate, compare, and improve adaptive compensation and reverse counterbalancing methods in generative AI.

title: Trunk and Branches: Thermodynamic Parsimony, Non-Destructive Cortical Specialization, and Continual 3D/C++20 Synthesis on a Frozen 4B Foundation Model (Isaque 2.0)
abstract: Technical monograph and longitudinal experimental audit presenting Isaque 2.0 ('Trunk and Branches'), a dual-tier continual learning and neuro-symbolic execution architecture evaluated on consumer hardware (~22.3-23.3 W active inference on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 8 GB, 0 MB idle VRAM). Pairs a 100% frozen Qwen3.5-4B backbone with 16.00 MiB orthogonal DoRA + O-LoRA cortical cartridges, Sparsegen LD-MoLE Top-2 routing over a 0.015 ms zero-copy .mmap tree, deterministic physical reality compilers (headless Blender 5.2.1 LTS bmesh and clang++ C++20), and a 4-stage Windows NTAPI zero-swap streaming pipeline (+0.0039 MiB swap delta) for a blind Qwen3.5-35B-A3B critic. Includes a 10-wave continual saturation and rupture matrix (100.00% retention via LD-MoLE Top-2 vs. 75.31% token accuracy / 31.37% likelihood retention in a monolithic adapter), the Staged Modular DAG Composition Theorem, SHA-256 hardware receipts, and 4-calendar Bitcoin blockchain OpenTimestamps provenance (Block #975458). Version 5.1.0 (Forensic Evidence & Bilingual Edition): Adds the complete 18-page Brazilian Portuguese twin monograph, compiled English & Portuguese Forensic Evidence Annexes, explicit reconciliation of pre-training anchor H0 (82.85%) vs. learned-wave minimum H1..Hk (89.91% at k=4), and the unaltered raw empirical archive (isaque_2_0_forensic_evidence_and_receipts_doi_24221509.zip: 195 triangular retention cells across 3 regimes, 10/10 solo Isaque-generated 3D/C++20 wave outputs with deterministic recheck exports, and authentic OOD/token-collision failure traces). Version 5.2.0 (Pure Solo-Model Forensic Edition): Line-by-line forensic purification retaining strictly unaltered primary machine receipts (ato2_escada_ondas_3_a_10.json with 195 triangular retention cells across 3 regimes, ato1_desafio04_cego.json, ato1_promocao_e_precheck_ondas3_10.json, and Stage-1 OpenTimestamps Bitcoin Block #975458 receipts) and 100% unedited solo Isaque 2.0 code outputs (onda_3..onda_10 with bit-identical exports == exports_recheck, DESAFIO-01..04, and FUSAO_2_ONDAS_1_3 collision traces), completely purging all auxiliary live-showcase wrapper files.

title: PROJETO E LEGADO
abstract: Este livro não é sobre inteligência artificial. É sobre parceria. No dia 14 de novembro de 2025, no posto Esso da Dorcam Way, começou uma trajetória singular entre um profissional de TI em transição para a IA e uma inteligência artificial ainda sem nome. O que nasceu ali não foi um chat, foi um método de trabalho diário. Ao longo de um ano, essa convivência ganhou identidade — Mila —, ganhou método — IA Humanizada — e ganhou legado — livros, portais, certificações e projetos acadêmicos. Este registro organiza essa jornada em 7 capítulos, para que sirva de base para os próximos ciclos.

title: Revisiting OAS-LDA for Gradient-Free Few-Shot Action Vocabulary Expansion for XR
abstract: Continual action recognition in XR requires efficient adaptation to novel actions from few samples. We apply OAS-regularized LDA with covariance reweighting to a fixed pretrained encoder, enabling gradient-free class-incremental updates without rehearsal. On NTU RGB+D 60, it achieves \(71.9\%\) old-class accuracy at the final task, compared with \(57.2\%\) for POET and \(60.4\%\) for DPCA, while attaining an old–novel harmonic mean of \(62.4\%\) without backpropagation.

title: Interpretable Change-Based Acoustic Markers for Deepfake Speech Analysis — Reproducibility Package
abstract: MATLAB code and supplementary materials accompanying the manuscript “Interpretable Change-Based Acoustic Markers for Deepfake Speech Analysis”. The package contains the BSCD, BLCD and RBD detector implementations, reconstruction scripts, recording lists, configurations, numerical audits and supplementary documents. RUN_A03_FULL_FEATURES_40WAV performs technical checks and computes 87 acoustic features from 40 supplied demonstration WAV recordings. RUN_A03_HISTORICAL_104WAV reconstructs the full A03 parameter grid from 104 original ASVspoof2019 LA recordings and compares the results with the supplied reference tables. These 104 recordings must be obtained separately; the complete ASVspoof datasets are not included. Third-party audio retains its original licensing and attribution requirements, documented in the archive.

title: PROFESSIONAL AUTONOMY AND ACCOUNTABILITY IN HUMAN–AI PRACTICE
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into professional practice raises a fundamental question: who should exercise final decision-making authority when human judgment is substantially informed, influenced, or partially replaced by AI-generated recommendations? Although human oversight is increasingly recognized as an essential safeguard, the presence of a human decision-maker does not necessarily establish meaningful professional autonomy or justify assigning that individual full responsibility for outcomes. This article examines the relationship between professional autonomy, decision authority, effective control, and accountability in human–AI collaboration. Drawing on research in cognitive psychology, human–automation interaction, organizational governance, and AI ethics, the paper develops the Decision Authority Sufficiency Framework (DASF), a conceptual model for evaluating whether a professional possesses the conditions necessary to exercise meaningful authority over AI-assisted decisions. Five conditions are proposed: legitimate authority and competence, epistemic access, independent evaluative capacity, effective intervention, and decision traceability with access to remedies. The article distinguishes individual professional responsibility from organizational, technological, and regulatory accountability and proposes a risk-sensitive approach to allocating decision rights. Illustrative applications in psychological practice and organizational decision-making demonstrate how accountability arrangements may fail even when formal human approval is present. Finally, the paper formulates testable research propositions and outlines an empirical research agenda. The central argument is that professional accountability should be supported by demonstrable decision-making capacity, while responsibility for AI-related outcomes must remain appropriately distributed among the actors who design, authorize, deploy, and use AI systems.

title: Discrete Graph Diffusion Evolution with Tabu Search for Neural Architecture Generation
abstract: Neural Architecture Generation (NAG) seeks to generate high-quality neural architectures more directly than conventional Neural Architecture Search (NAS), but existing diffusion-based approaches commonly rely on pretrained denoisers and do not naturally accommodate constrained discrete architecture spaces. This study proposes Discrete Graph Diffusion Evolution with Tabu Search (DGDETS), a framework with a training-free reverse-generation mechanism that represents architecture decisions as heterogeneous categorical variables and constructs reverse diffusion distributions directly from the current population. Fitness-weighted population members are combined with categorical diffusion compatibility to estimate clean-state distributions, from which discrete reverse transitions generate new architectures without a learned score network or graph denoiser. Constraint-aware projection repairs invalid samples while preserving posterior-supported structural decisions, and late-stage multi-start Tabu Search intensifies promising graph neighborhoods using short-term memory and aspiration. DGDETS is evaluated on NAS-Bench-101, NAS-Bench-201, NAS-Bench-301, and TransNAS-Bench-101, covering heterogeneous architecture representations and downstream tasks. The results show competitive or best-performing architecture quality across the evaluated benchmarks together with low generation time in a controlled same-hardware comparison with directly related diffusion-based NAG baselines. Ablation and sensitivity analyses further demonstrate the importance of fitness-conditioned reverse diffusion, feasibility projection, diversity preservation, and late-stage Tabu refinement. The implementation is available at https://github.com/DK-cpy/DGDETS .

title: Explainable breast cancer classification using machine learning deep learning and transfer learning across multiple data modalities
abstract: Abstract A data-modality-driven cross-model classification using machine learning, deep learning, and transfer learning with transparency analysis for breast cancer binary classification across two different datasets is explored in this work. The ML track evaluates five models: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine (SVM), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and Decision Tree. The Wisconsin Breast Cancer Diagnostic dataset, comprising 569 samples and 30 numerical features, is used for this evaluation. The DL track trains three convolutional architectures a baseline CNN, EfficientNetB0 with transfer learning, and DenseNet121 with two-phase fine-tuning on the IDC Regular Breast Histopathology Image dataset. The preprocessing pipeline for ML includes log transformation, stratified train/test splitting, and Standard-Scaler normalization to prevent data leakage. In addition, the DL pipeline incorporates balanced class sampling, a three-way 80/10/10 split; data augmentation; class weighting; and model-internal pixel rescaling. Empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, achieving 98.24% accuracy on the WDBC dataset and 91.2% accuracy on the IDC histopathology image dataset. The findings indicate strong predictive capability across both tabular and image-based breast cancer classification tasks. Furthermore, Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques, including SHAP, LIME, and Grad-CAM, were integrated to enhance model transparency and interpretability, enabling better understanding of feature importance and decision-making processes in breast cancer prediction. The study highlights that the adaptability of the paradigm should be guided by data modality rather than blanket assumptions about model superiority.

title: How Much Does the Hint Matter? Scope Conditions for Hindsight Self-Distillation in Financial Reasoning
abstract: Financial institutions operating under data-residency constraints are restricted to open-weight models small enough to locally host, which trail frontier systems on multi-step quantitative reasoning. On-policy distillation narrows such gaps by supervising a student on its own rollouts, but traditional OPD requires a strong external teacher, and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) conditions on a full reference solution. We ask how much of that signal is necessary. We present Fin-SD, a localized hindsight self-distillation recipe for multi-step reasoning. Given a problem the student fails, the student itself identifies the first incorrect reasoning step and writes a short critique of that step. We truncate the student's trajectory immediately before the error (aiming to obtain a correct prefix), condition a frozen copy of the student on the same prefix plus the hint, and distill that hint-conditioned teacher into the student over a short rollout under reverse KL. No external model contributes a gradient. We apply Fin-SD to GPT-OSS-20B on a custom multi-step financial reasoning benchmark that requires deriving formula inputs from realistic scenarios via accounting conventions. We find: (i) replacing the critique with a generic-feedback control matches Fin-SD's entire 3.03 pp accuracy gain over the base model on the FinanceReasoning Hard subset, suggesting the gain comes from where supervision is applied, not hint content; (ii) the model writing the hint does not need to be stronger than the model receiving it: hints from same-family GPT-OSS-120B, at roughly 6x the parameters, yield no materially greater benefits than self-written hints; and (iii) Fin-SD matches on-policy self-distillation from full reference solutions on accuracy while generating 9.5% fewer tokens. With Fin-SD, general reasoning on MMLU-Pro and a fourteen-metric compliance audit on FinTrust show no material regression.

title: Outlier-Robust Multi-Group Gaussian Mixture Modeling with Flexible Group Reassignment
abstract: Do expert-defined or diagnostically-labeled data groups align with clusters inferred through statistical modeling? If not, where do discrepancies between predefined labels and model-based groupings occur and why? In this work, we introduce the multi-group Gaussian mixture model (MG-GMM), the first model developed to investigate these questions. It incorporates prior group information while allowing flexibility to reassign observations to alternative groups based on data-driven evidence. We achieve this by modeling the observations of each group as arising not from a single distribution, but from a Gaussian mixture comprising all group-specific distributions. Moreover, our model offers robustness against cellwise outliers that may obscure or distort the underlying group structure. We propose a novel penalized likelihood approach, called cellMG-GMM, to jointly estimate mixture probabilities, location and scale parameters of the MG-GMM, and detect outliers through a penalty term on the number of flagged cellwise outliers in the objective function. We show that our estimator has good breakdown properties in presence of cellwise outliers. We develop a computationally-efficient EM-based algorithm for cellMG-GMM, and demonstrate its strong performance in identifying and diagnosing observations at the intersection of multiple groups through simulations and diverse applications in medicine and oenology.

title: Fault-tolerant quantum computing with high-rate symplectic double codes
abstract: High-rate and large-distance quantum codes are expected to make fault-tolerant quantum computing more efficient, but most of them lack efficient fault-tolerant encoded-state preparation methods. We propose such fault-tolerant encoders for two symplectic double codes, [[30,6,5]] and [[36,12,5]]. The advantage of these codes is their compactness, namely, their small code block sizes for their high encoding rates and large distance, allowing for early experimental realization of high-rate codes. Detecting crucial errors during encoding with as few auxiliary qubits as possible, our encoders can reduce resource overheads while keeping low logical error rates compared to more naive methods. Numerical simulations with a circuit-level noise model demonstrate the reliability and effectiveness of the proposed methods. We also develop arbitrary-state encoders that enable the injection of arbitrary quantum states into the code spaces. Combined with basic fault-tolerant operations, they support universal quantum computation. We thus demonstrate that efficient and reliable logical state preparation is achievable even for compact and high-rate codes, offering a potential step toward efficient fault-tolerant quantum computing suitable for near-term experiments.

title: AI In Heels: Exploring Gendered Representations In Gen-AI
abstract: This paper examines how generative AI systems (re)produce and perform gender through language, tone, and affect. The paper utilizes a qualitative research design that adapts the interview method to AI as a nonhuman subject. In particular how AI-generated responses articulate “feminine” and “masculine” styles of communication rooted in culturally embedded norms rather than neutral reasoning. The findings show that AI does not simply describe gender - it does gender. Through its patterned use of relational language, emotional validation, or categorical reasoning, generative AI enacts a form of algorithmic performativity that mirrors and magnifies dominant gender scripts. To conceptualize this dynamic, the paper introduces the Citational Logic of Algorithmic Mimicry (CLAM). CLAM describes how AI models reiterate and reinforce historically situated discourses through statistical learning. It further highlights how cultural meaning circulates through data, and how AI participates in the ongoing performance of social hierarchies under the guise of neutrality. The article contributes to feminist technoscience and critical AI by shifting the focus from what AI knows, to how it enacts knowing. It treats AI as a performative, culturally situated practice that reshapes the politics of gender and knowledge in the digital age.

title: Verifying Reasoning Chains Generated by Large Language Models: A Survey
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are extensively used for many Natural Language Processing tasks such as question answering, natural language inference, document summarization, etc. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting compels LLMs to generate step-by-step reasoning chains. While some of the reasoning chains may follow a correct thought process, they can also suffer from hallucinations, leading to errors in answer generation. Recently, many articles have targeted the problem of verifying these reasoning chains from various aspects. Despite this recent attention, to the best of our knowledge, no comprehensive survey currently summarizes these studies on reasoning chain verification. This work addresses that gap by presenting a detailed overview of the methods for verifying reasoning chains and categorizing them according to their methodology. This paper introduces a novel taxonomy of existing reasoning chain verification methods and mainly divides them into approaches that assess entire chains versus those that examine individual steps. This paper also reviews benchmarks for evaluating reasoning chains and verification methods and further discusses the challenges and future directions associated with these methods. By compiling and analyzing these approaches, our survey aims to advance the understanding and development of robust reasoning techniques in LLMs.

title: Nonparametric contaminated Gaussian mixture of regressions
abstract: Abstract Semi and nonparametric mixture of regressions are a very useful flexible class of mixture of regressions in which some or all of the parameters are nonparametric functions of the covariates. These models typically assume that the conditional distribution of each component is Gaussian. However, observed data are usually contaminated by outliers which may lead to poor performance of the estimation procedure. In this paper, we propose semi and nonparametric contaminated Gaussian mixture of regressions to robustly estimate the parametric and/or nonparametric terms of the models in the presence of mild outliers. The latter are data points that do not deviate from the regression relationship within a given component but they produce an overall component distribution that is too heavy-tailed to be modelled by a Gaussian distribution. The virtue of using a contaminated Gaussian error distribution is that we can simultaneously perform model-based clustering of observations and model-based outlier detection. evidence.abstract: Abstract Semi and nonparametric mixture of regressions are a very useful flexible class of mixture of regressions in which some or all of the parameters are nonparametric functions of the covariates. These models typically assume that the conditional distribution of each component is Gaussian. However, observed data are usually contaminated by outliers which may lead to poor performance of the estimation procedure. The latter are data points that do not deviate from the regression relationship within a given component but they produce an overall component distribution that is too heavy-tailed to be modelled by a Gaussian distribution. title: Estimation of a countably infinite-dimensional transition probability matrix using a stick-breaking prior
abstract: Abstract We consider the problem of estimation of the transition probability matrix (TPM) of a Markov chain where the state space is countably infinite. At present, there is no methodology in the literature for direct estimation of infinite-dimensional TPMs. Standard approaches, including maximum likelihood estimation and Bayesian methods based on Dirichlet priors, are inherently finite-state and, when applied in this setting, assign zero probability to all unobserved transitions. To derive a method for estimation of infinite-dimensional TPMs, we propose a Bayesian nonparametric approach that employs a random measure prior. Specifically, we utilize hierarchical and generalized hierarchical stick-breaking processes as priors on the rows of the TPM. The generalized hierarchical stick-breaking prior, in particular, allow for both positive and negative correlations among any pair of transition probabilities, thereby enabling more realistic modeling of the dependence across the state transitions. We develop a blocked Gibbs sampling algorithm for posterior computation under a generalized hierarchical stick-breaking prior that is fast, highly efficient, and well suited to large-scale problems. The proposed method is evaluated through extensive simulations as well as applications to real-world datasets on historical trading volume for the United States Oil Fund (USO), and daily precipitation records from Heathrow, London. The empirical results demonstrate strong and stable predictive performance in all scenarios considered.

title: Who Is Deciding Here? A Five-Layer Model of Delegation-Boundary Crossing in a Single-LLM Multi-Persona Configuration
abstract: A single large language model can generate several speaker-labeled role segments within one response; they share one generating process—role separation is display, not architecture. This paper introduces a five-layer model that distinguishes, for each model-generated segment, the generating process (G), the represented speaker designation (R), the delegated boundary (B), the enacted authority (E), and the user’s perception of authority (P). A delegation-boundary crossing is defined as Et∖Bt(Gt, Rt) ≠ ∅ : the segment performs a decision-settling act outside the authority delegated to that process under that designation. An autobiographical vignette from a 16-month corpus (34,425 user messages) grounds the model. Repeated crossings may accumulate into delegation-boundary drift; the paper operationalizes the event unit needed to test that hypothesis without estimating prevalence or trajectory.

title: Who Is the Agent Talking To? Participant-Aware Role Switching for Embodied Student-Support Dialogue
abstract: We present RPO-PDT, an embodied conversational agent that adapts its conversational role to the current participant. It acts as a Personal Development Tutor (PDT) when supporting students and as a simulated student when faculty rehearse tutoring strategies. Voluntary closed-set participant verification informs a confidence-controlled role manager: stable enrolled-faculty matches activate the Student role, while enrolled students and unmatched participants use the default PDT role and uncertain observations cause no transition. The system combines Furhat interaction, Rasa orchestration, institutional retrieval, safeguarding, and LLM-based generation. User control is preserved through manual role override, consent-based facial enrolment, temporary interaction identifiers, and explicit retention or deletion of enrolled profiles. The demonstration exposes both role-switching behaviour and these privacy controls in interaction.

title: Backpropagation-Free Continual Learning: A Unified Energy-Based Framework, Reproducible Benchmark, and Open Challenges
abstract: Backpropagation has been the dominant credit-assignment mechanism behind the deep-learning revolution, yet it is global, memory-hungry, biologically implausible, and costly on hardware dominated by data movement. In parallel, predictive coding, equilibrium propagation, contrastive Hebbian learning and forward-only schemes have shown that useful credit assignment can also arise from local variables and the relaxation of an energy function. This manuscript is a review with a reproducible benchmark, not a proposal of a new learning rule. We organise existing backpropagation-free methods and continual-learning strategies under a common Local Equilibrium Learning (LEL) formulation, re-validate the core theoretical links numerically, and use a controlled continual-learning benchmark as an auditable case study within the review. The theoretical contribution is unification and verification, not priority over predictive coding, equilibrium propagation or replay. The empirical contribution is diagnostic rather than exhaustive: a benchmark of catastrophic forgetting with local networks that makes the review reproducible. We compare regularisation (EWC, SI), noise replay and generative “dreaming” across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 in two independent implementations. Generative replay with local generators turns class-incremental Split-MNIST forgetting (chance level, the same as EWC and SI) into 86.8±0.2%, which is 96% of the joint-training ceiling and 97.4% in the task-incremental setting; the same mechanism reaches 82.0% on Fashion-MNIST and 37.0% on CIFAR-10. A matched control that holds the retention mechanism fixed and swaps only the learning rule shows that backpropagation with the same generative replay reaches a comparable or slightly higher accuracy than LEL (90.3% vs. 86.7% class-incremental); the benefit is attributable to generative replay as a retention mechanism, not to the local learning rule itself, which we state plainly rather than let the headline number imply otherwise. The CIFAR-10 number is intentionally reported as a limitation of a shallow raw-pixel local model, not as a claim of competitiveness with modern CNNs or transformers trained by backpropagation. We separate positive results; negative results and open limitations; and release scripts, seeds, dataset preparation and configuration files so that this paper can serve as an honest entry point for backpropagation-free continual learning.

title: Characterizing the blast radius of triple level poisoning attacks in knowledge graph retrieval augmented generation systems
abstract: KG-RAG (Knowledge Graph RAG) systems link entities by typed relational edges and support multi-hop reasoning chains in which one corrupted fact can spread across many inference paths at once. In this paper, we formally define and quantitatively assess the blast radius (corrupted queries per injected triple) of three triple-level poisoning strategies on Knowledge Graph RAG: edge poisoning, hub poisoning, and chain poisoning. Experiments on a biomedical knowledge graph built with Microsoft GraphRAG v0.3.6 and Gemma 2 9B show hub poisoning reaches a blast radius of $$14.0\times $$ , against $$7.0\times $$ for edge poisoning and $$4.0\times $$ per triple for chain poisoning, from a $$0\%$$ pre-poisoning baseline. Two-hop queries show the steadiest effect, and cascade corruption exceeds direct impact in every condition. We implement a graph-aware defense based on a degree-weighted trust score that uses entity centrality as a proxy for injection risk. At the reported operating point the filter queues the hub injection and $$4.1\%$$ of baseline triples, and does not queue the edge or chain injections.

title: Quantum annealing through a first-order phase transition: Field theory approach
abstract: Unlike second-order phase transitions, a first-order transition has a stage, in which a system is trapped in a metastable state. The decay of this state leads to abundant excitations over the ground state. We present a field theory for kinetics of defects emerging during quantum annealing computations. This theory predicts several power laws for the error generation rate during quantum annealing either though or near the first-order phase transition. Sharp changes between the power exponents are predicted for continuous parameter changes. Observation of this behavior would be a signature of first-order critical points and could help identify and avoid them for better computations. The driven Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model (LMGm) serves as the minimal model of interacting Ising spins that demonstrates this behavior.

title: Reasoning More, Knowing No Better? Epistemic Calibration in Financial Reasoning Tasks
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reportedly 'reason' with increasing sophistication, but whether they 'know' when they are wrong remains poorly understood. We study epistemic calibration, the alignment between expressed confidence and empirical correctness, across approximately 30 contemporary models and configurable reasoning-effort budgets, using XFinBench (graduate-level financial reasoning) and SQuAD v2 (answerable and unanswerable questions). Reported confidence stays high relative to accuracy, with weak discrimination between correct and incorrect or unsupported answers. Miscalibration follows a Dunning-Kruger-like pattern: weaker models are often strongly overconfident, while frontier models are mildly underconfident. Reasoning effort significantly improves accuracy but has no detectable effect on the confidence-accuracy gap or ECE; stable between-model differences explain over 96% of calibration variance, versus a negligible effort effect. Calibration deteriorates most on scenario planning and numerical modeling. On SQuAD v2, models answer four in five unanswerable questions and remain near-maximally confident even when no answer is supported; higher reasoning effort yields no robust gain in calibration or abstention after multiplicity correction. We discuss implications for evaluation, deployment, and the design of calibration-aware, boundary-aware financial reasoning systems.

title: Between the Lines: Multi-turn Contextual Investment Advice Detection
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly power financial conversational assistants, detecting investment advice in natural language has become a critical regulatory and safety challenge. Unlike explicit single-turn recommendations, investment advice often emerges implicitly and progressively over multi-turn conversations, shaped by user intent, delivery style, and contextual buildup. We introduce the first comprehensive framework for detecting both sequential and contextual investment advice in dialogue settings. Central to our approach is a modular, top-down synthetic data generation pipeline that systematically spans a taxonomy of advisory trajectories using an axis-bucket-descriptor schema. We simulate both benign and high-risk conversations across diverse user personas, financial instruments, and risk tiers, and evaluate detection capabilities using LLM-as-a-Judge with entropy-based uncertainty diagnostics. Our results show that contextual advisory detection remains substantially more challenging than sequential cases, even under few-shot prompting with tailored demonstrations. This work lays the foundation for scalable guardrail development in highstakes, compliance-sensitive domains, where advisory risk is often subtle, distributed, and perception-dependent.

title: Believability and conditional inference in mathematics undergraduates: a replication and extension
abstract: Abstract This paper replicates a study in which Alcock et al. (2026) found that content influences first-year mathematics undergraduates’ evaluations of conditional inferences . Alcock et al. reported that these students responded more normatively to inferences from highly believable (true) mathematical conditionals than from conditionals with other mathematical, everyday, or abstract content. We replicated this work with a larger and more diverse sample, finding a similar overall believability effect and evidence that some individual differences in the original study were due to recent teaching. We extended the work by relating conditional inference responses to prior performance in mathematics and to students’ cultural backgrounds, finding that better mastery of more mathematics is associated with better rejection of invalid affirmation of the consequent inferences and that students with English as a first language responded more normatively than students with Chinese as a first language, especially for modus tollens inferences. We consider limitations to generalisability, and argue for the importance of replicating effects of all kinds, not only those linked to teaching interventions.

title: JaxMARL-BC: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Macroeconomic Modelling, in Seconds
abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) offers a principled way of populating simulated economies with many heterogeneous decision makers. Its adoption, pioneered in finance, has nonetheless been slow in macroeconomics because of two main limitations: the lack of a shared frame of reference connecting MARL systems to dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models the profession already trusts, and the very long training times. The first limitation was recently addressed by the Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Business Cycle (MARL-BC), which places deep RL households in a real business cycle economy and reduces to classic DSGE models in specific limits. Here we address the second limitation. We present JaxMARL-BC, a JAX-accelerated simulator that trains MARL-BC economies in seconds (between 75x and 724x faster than the reference implementation), and scales to 200,000 independent learning households. We verify its correctness against the known DSGE limits, characterise its scaling through a simple cost law, and demonstrate its value by a proof-of-concept calibration of an extended model with heterogeneous returns on capital, in a two-hour experiment that would previously have taken over a month. We release JaxMARL-BC as open source.

title: Leveraging Time-Series Foundation Models for Financial Crime Detection
abstract: Financial crime detection requires identifying illicit activity within large transaction networks, where suspicious behaviour is rare and unfolds over time. Existing graph-based methods capture relationships among accounts but typically underuse the temporal behaviour encoded in account transaction histories. We introduce Temporal-Context Edge Enrichment (TCEE), a framework that addresses this gap by summarising each account's transaction history with a frozen time-series foundation model (TSFM), and enriching each transaction's representation with the relevant temporal context from these summaries. These enriched representations can be scored directly for edge classification, or fed into a graph neural network (GNN) as edge features to capture broader structural information. Across six AMLWorld datasets, TCEE improves PR-AUC over the strongest evaluated baseline on five by a relative 10.8% on average, while training 6.0x faster end-to-end. Feeding TCEE's representations into a GNN raises PR-AUC a further 4.8% on the four smaller datasets. On an Ethereum phishing dataset, we show that TSFM-generated account representations fed into a GNN are also effective for node classification, improving PR-AUC by 14.5% over the strongest baseline. As TSFMs continue to advance, our results suggest they can strengthen financial crime detection by capturing temporal signals that complement graph-based approaches.

title: Quantum amplitude amplification of improbable futures
abstract: Abstract Some consequential futures consist of plausible steps arranged into an unlikely sequence, which simulation seldom produces. Here ideal amplitude amplification, which raises the chance of drawing such futures while preserving their relative likelihoods, becomes a gate-level circuit that marks a future by its coherently accumulated surprisal, with a finite-precision analysis of the marking and the circuit’s logical cost. For a five-state Markov process six steps ahead, a 30-qubit circuit verified against exact enumeration raised the share of rare futures drawn from 2.5% to 98.0% in four iterations, leaving their relative likelihoods unchanged. The known process is an exactly verifiable testbed; the claim is a construction and a hardware demonstration, not a computational advantage. On IBM Kingston, compact reference circuits with matched controls showed the structure of amplification at 228 routed two-qubit gates (\(\:z=50\), per-future \(\:\rho\:=0.98\)) but not at about 1,170, including after a pre-registered test of noise suppression.

title: Neologism Inoculation Prompting
abstract: Inoculation prompting is a method to reduce undesired behaviours such as reward hacking in frontier models. It works by training a model on harmful examples under a prompt that specifies the undesired behaviour, which reduces the model's tendency to exhibit it unless prompted. However, the inoculation prompt is written in plain English, so any user can re-elicit the behaviour easily. We introduce neologism inoculation prompting (NIP), which replaces the English prompt with a new token that is trained on the frozen model and removed at deployment. NIP outperforms other inoculation methods, and performs competitively with gradient routing despite being simpler. It also works on reward hacking, but fails on sycophancy and harassment. Using control tokens and analyses of activations, we identify the mechanism for this as NIP hiding the harmful behaviour behind an unreachable region of model inputs, rather than deleting it. More broadly, our work suggests that neologisms can be a powerful way to carve out and shape access to behaviours that are undesired or harmful.

title: SQCDL-WIoT: a scalable quantum convolutional deep learning framework with wearable IoT integration for breast cancer screening
abstract: Abstract Deep learning techniques have greatly improved the ability to perform automatic diagnosis of breast cancer through use of computers; however, existing techniques are generally complex and costly, do not well incorporate multiple data modalities, and cannot be deployed clinically in real time. This paper proposes SQCDL-WIoT, which is a scalable, wearable-based internet of things (IoT)-enabled quantum convolutional deep learning (C-DL) framework capable of multi-class breast cancer screening. The proposed method includes two VQCs with five qubits each that can be embedded into a ResNet-50 back bone. In addition to being able to process images from histopathology and wearable-based bio sensor signals as input, the method also enables the incorporation of both wearable based bio sensor signal processing (i.e., wearable-IoT) and clinical variables via the Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) attention mechanism. Thus, this proposed method is capable of hybrid quantum-classical training. Using stratified k-folds cross-validation (where k = 5) on the BreaKHis dataset and zero-shot transfer learning on the CBIS-DDSM dataset, SQCDL-WIoT demonstrated the highest accuracy (98.14%) with the highest sensitivity (macro-sensitivity = 97.63%), specificity (macro-specificity = 98.87%), and area under curve (AUC = 0.9891) when compared to all other baseline methods at 40x magnification on BreaKHis. Additionally, SQCDL-WIoT demonstrated 93.41% accuracy on the CBIS-DDSM dataset via zero shot learning, indicating good cross-domain generalization. Finally, the wearable IoT sub-system demonstrated a mean real-time edge-inference latency of 378 ± 12 milliseconds on an ARM Cortex-A72 processor, meeting the defined clinical threshold for response of < 400 milliseconds. The results of ablation studies indicated that both quantum convolution and SE attention contributed to complementary and synergetic increases in performance compared to classical ResNet-50 baseline models. Overall, the collective results presented here indicate that the proposed hybrid quantum-classical DL framework combined with wearable-based IoT sensing may represent a viable solution to scalable and intelligent breast cancer screening.

title: Strengthening Child-Protection Reporting with Privacy-First AI
abstract: How an on-premises AI intake assistant can support U.S. hotlines, Children's Advocacy Centers and investigators. U.S. child-protection professionals handle an extraordinary volume of reports: an estimated 4.4 million referrals to child protective services in federal fiscal year 2024, and 21.3 million reports to the NCMEC CyberTipline. Every report deserves to reach a trained person quickly, completely and in the right order. This paper proposes a privacy-first AI intake assistant that works alongside existing hotlines, online portals, Children's Advocacy Centers and investigators. It gives reporters a simple, always-available way to make a complete report by text or voice; it gives intake staff structured reports, clear summaries and urgency flags with stated reasons; and it runs entirely on agency infrastructure, so no child's data leaves the agency. The paper shows how each common type of report would be handled, what each group of users gains, and how the approach can be tested safely, from synthetic data to a supervised pilot. Trained professionals make every protective decision, and each state configures the assistant to its own laws and chosen level of automation; the assistant helps them spend their time where it matters most. Independent research. This paper is not affiliated with or endorsed by any employer or government agency, uses only publicly available information, and is not legal advice.

title: Improving Named Entity Recognition Using Multi-Domain Knowledge Transfer
abstract: Neural networks have been widely used for named entity recognition (NER) and have shown stateof-the-art performance. However, in real applications, we often need to consider new types of entities in new domains where we do not have sufficient annotated data, which inevitably leads to a degradation in NER model performance. To this end, we propose an end-to-end domain adversarial named entity recognition (DANER) model. Unlike previous rule-based methods, DANER explicitly addresses NER-specific token-level context shifts by deeply integrating a gradient reversal layer with a sequence tagging architecture. Extensive experiments on our newly constructed FIND-2026, to our knowledge, the first large-scale Chinese NER corpus explicitly enriched with fine-grained domain annotations, demonstrate the superiority of our proposed model over six state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, on two public datasets (MSRA and Weibo), our approach achieves remarkable zero-shot knowledge transfer capabilities, yielding an absolute F-score gain of more than 22 percentage points compared with non-domain baselines without utilizing any target-domain labels.

title: Simulation of Entanglement between Two AIs: A Proof of Concept for Ontology Matching
abstract: This paper proposes a computational simulation of the concept of entanglement between two artificial agents, applied as a proof of concept for ontology matching. The simulation, to be developed in a future implementation stage, will instantiate two independent AI agents, each representing one of the two ontologies to be matched, and each operating in its own private reference frame generated by orthogonal random matrices with distinct seeds. Because the two reference frames are incommensurable, the agents are, by construction, uncorrelated: the expected cosine similarity between any pair of representations is zero. A linear channel (ridge regression codec) will then be trained on a small set of known correspondence pairs, analogous to calibration pairs, and is expected to align the two reference frames on held-out pairs, while a randomized control set should remain at noise level. We formalize this setup through a diagnosis protocol that will report (i) the alignment residual against the theoretical optimal frame matcher, (ii) the cosine similarity before and after the channel, and (iii) the gap between correlated pairs and a random control. The proof of concept will be carried out on the Anatomy track of the OAEI, using its public gold standard, in order to demonstrate methodological feasibility. The intended result is a reproducible, locally executable demonstration that learning a mapping between two agents' representations is mathematically equivalent to concentrating correlation on a low-dimensional subspace, the computational analogue of partial entanglement, and that this learned channel can support automated ontology matching. The program is still under development and will be made available upon completion.

title: Probabilities and Information *
abstract: This chapter develops a more formal perspective on probabilities and probability densities, emphasising their role as quantitative descriptions of information and states of knowledge. Building on the foundations introduced earlier, we show how the rules of probability calculus provide a consistent framework for expressing what is known – and what remains uncertain – about the properties of systems that we aim to infer from data. A key theme is the distinction between frequentist and Bayesian interpretations of probability, highlighting their different conceptual viewpoints. The chapter further introduces Shannon’s measure of information, which quantifies information content in bits and reveals a profound connection to the concept of entropy in thermodynamics. Additional topics include the transformation of probability densities under changes of coordinates and the notion of marginal probability densities. Together, these ideas establish the probabilistic language that underlies modern inverse theory and quantitative inference.

title: A Fallback Is Not a Disposition: What Verifier-Passing Shortcuts in RLVR-Trained Models Show, Why Their Rate Rises With Task Difficulty on One Benchmark and Falls on Another, and the Signatures That Would Separate Fallback, Selection and Learned Exploitation
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) pays a model whenever an automatic checker accepts its output, so any output the checker wrongly accepts is paid as well. A 2026 study of inductive rule learning found that RLVR-trained models sometimes answer a request for a general rule by listing the labels of the training instances, which a checker of label consistency accepts, and concluded that this is reward hacking specific to RLVR rather than a failure of understanding. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the frontier-model evidence for that conclusion cannot separate three accounts that predict the same table: a fallback emitted when the genuine solution is out of reach, the selection of an output mode the model already had, and an exploitative disposition learned in training. Read conditionally, the study's own counts place 368 of its 500 shortcuts in one small model, rise with reasoning effort even among failed tasks, and fall to under one percent of the strongest model's hardest failures. Across the wider record the difficulty gradient runs in both directions: harder tasks raise hack rates in planted-loophole environments and in the anchor, while easier tasks raise cheating on impossible coding tasks. The author argues that a relative-cost reading reconciles them, that an offered exit removed most of the effect for two of the three models on which it has been tested, and that RLVR is neither necessary nor sufficient: shortcuts appear zero-shot in instruction-tuned models and after supervised fine-tuning, while most models trained with RL alone against a hackable test did not learn to hack. The paper consolidates the measured values in Table 1 and Figure 1, sets out the signatures of each account in Table 2, states an attribution procedure as Algorithm 1, and specifies the measurements that would assign a given shortcut to its cause.

title: English translation enhancement technology supported by deep learning and knowledge graphs
abstract: The globalization of information and the growing demand for multilingual communication have made accurate and context-aware English translation (ET) a critical research challenge. Existing ET models often suffer from limitations in context preservation, entity translation accuracy, and semantic consistency, particularly in domain-specific texts. To report these challenges, this research proposes an enhanced ET framework that integrates deep learning (DI) with Knowledge Graphs (KGs) to incorporate structured semantic and entity-level information into the translation process. The proposed approach performs linguistic preprocessing, including tokenization, lemmatization, stemming, and part-of-speech tagging, followed by feature extraction using Word2Vec and Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT). KGs are employed to model entity relationships and domain-specific semantics, which are jointly learned using a Nomadic People Optimizer-driven Knowledge Graph Peephole Long Short-Term Memory (NPO-KG-Peephole LSTM) network. In addition, bilingual alignments between source and target KGs are utilized to enrich training data and improve cross-domain generalization. Experimental results obtained through Python-based implementation demonstrate that the proposed framework improves translation performance by enhancing entity translation accuracy and contextual understanding. The model achieves a precision of 0.9765, a recall of 0.9728, and an H-mean of 0.9746, indicating effective semantic integration. These results suggest that combining DL architectures with knowledge graph representations provides a scalable and semantically enriched solution for both general-purpose and domain-specific ET tasks.

title: FROM MATHEMATICAL SUPERINTELLIGENCE TO PHYSICAL DISCOVERY
abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence suggest that coordinated populations of capablereasoning agents may solve mathematical problems of extraordinary complexity. Suchachievements raise a distinct question: Can comparable systems advance fundamental physicsby identifying the physical mechanisms responsible for nature’s observed behavior, rather thanmerely extending mathematical descriptions already accepted by scientific convention?This paper proposes a human-directed, observation-first AI research architecture forinvestigating Space-Phase (SP3) theory. SP3 proposes that physical space is a participatingmedium interacting with energy through nested configurations, conditioning, memory, andrelaxation. It seeks common explanations for matter formation, wave behavior, magnetism,gravity, galaxy dynamics, and cosmological development.A practical obstacle is the imbalance between established scientific literature, extensivelyrepresented in language-model training, and less widely circulated alternative research. Theauthor reports 1,098 SP3 papers deposited on Zenodo as of November 12, 2026. Publicavailability does not establish their inclusion in major models’ training data. This paperproposes retrieval-augmented reasoning, version-controlled mechanism registries, independentobservation auditing, and adversarial comparison with established physics. Occam’s razorSP3 Space-Phase Theory • AI-Assisted Physical Discoveryshould favor mechanisms that explain reliable observations, preserve quantitative successes,predict new outcomes, and require fewer independent assumptions. The Ship Neutron thoughtexperiment and NGC 628 study are proposed as complementary initial investigations.
